description:
Welcome to Orbitals! We are Passionate about using technology and data to tackle challenges in space.

Our interests include software development, artificial intelligence, data analysis and user experience design.

We welcome teammate with skills and interests in software development, artificial intelligence, data sciences and UI/UX design, healthcare, biomedical engineering or space science.
summary:
On a mission to Mars, a message to the flight surgeon takes about 20 minutes to arrive, and the answer takes another 20 minutes to come back. When something feels wrong, the crew has to act first and ask later. AstroVitals is a health app built for that gap.

Each morning it shows a crew member their body, their cabin air, and their radiation dose on one screen. Every reading is checked against their own usual range and sorted into one of six alert levels, from Normal to Emergency, each with clear steps for what to do next. At night and during spacewalks, minor items wait for a summary, so only urgent alerts get through.

It's built for life far from Earth, where help is always 20 minutes away.
details:
What it does

AstroVitals is the daily health check for the astronaut on a long mission. It's based around NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity and the closed cabin environment). Each reading is categorised into one of six levels (Normal, Monitor, Advisory, Action soon, Act now and Emergency) and each level tells the crew precisely what to do.

If blood oxygen drops to 87% the screen becomes a red checklist: initiate oxygen procedure, inform the Commander. Each step has to be acknowledged by the crew before the alert clears. If cabin CO₂ starts to rise then the only action is "Move to ventilated module". During a solar storm you get the radiation alert and that takes you straight to the shelter procedure.

How it works

We compare each reading against the crew member's own 14 day baseline rather than the population average and against the limits for wherever they are. You can switch between a space station, a lunar base, a transit vehicle and a Mars base and the advice changes with the distance. Near Earth it says "call the flight surgeon now". On the way to Mars it says "start with your crew then send one complete message". Messages to the ground go into a queue and wait until the next comms window.

Why it matters

The crew will always know what to do in the next five minutes and will have a clear record ready when the ground responds. Any health tool for deep space has to be built around the delay, not just the data.

What we thought about

- Every alert level has its own shape as well as its own colour so it's still useful for the colour blind crew and in low light.

- On a serious alert the first button is treatment not "re-measure". If you want to override an alert the app will ask you why.

- At night and during spacewalks the only alerts you get are the urgent ones. You don't need a 'sleep' reminder in the middle of an EVA.

- Badges are for logging, not for good numbers. We absolutely didn't want people hiding a bad reading to maintain their streak.

What makes it different

Most health apps operate on the premise that a doctor is one tap away. We started from the other end of the spectrum so the app changes how it talks to you depending on how far away from Earth you are.

How we built it

The app is in Dart and the backend is Python with FastAPI. For the demo we've created, every reading is generated from one of four scenarios that we've written up: a normal day, a strained week, a solar storm and a cabin air event. Lena Ortiz is a made up member of our test crew. The interactive demo we're sharing is a web prototype of the same design.
